DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 22SMCV02817    Hearing Date: September 14, 2026    Dept: 205

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District 

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

GREEN & MCCAHILL HOLDINGS LIMITED,   

  

Plaintiff, 

 

v. 

 

JCTLA INVESTMENT CORPORATION, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  22SMCV02817 

  

  Hearing Date: September 14, 2026 

 

  [TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: 

  PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO  

  STRIKE OR TAX DEFENDANT’S COSTS 

 

 

   

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This case arises from breach of a loan agreement.  Plaintiff alleges it loaned Defendant $529,000 bearing an interest of 8%, to be compounded annually.  Defendant repaid the principal amount but failed to pay the interest due.   

On June 10, 2026, Plaintiff filed a request for dismissal of its action, without prejudice.  On June 26, 2026, Defendant filed a memorandum of costs (summary) which sought $877.91 in filing and motion fees. 

This hearing is on Plaintiff’s motion to tax costs.  Plaintiff argues that because Defendant did not itemize the pleadings or motions that correlate with the filing or motion fees, and the charges appear to include more than filing or motion fees (as they include fractional dollar amounts), Defendant’s requested costs should be struck or taxed.   

The hearing was originally set August 21, 2026 but Defendant claimed it did not receive the motion.  Accordingly, the Court continued the hearing to this date, allowing Defendant to file an opposition by no later than August 28, 2026.  Defendant has now filed its opposition. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

Generally, a “prevailing party” is entitled to costs. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1032(b); Santisas v. Goodin (1998) 17 Cal.4th 599, 606.).  “A prevailing party who claims costs must serve and file a memorandum of costs within 15 days after the date of mailing of the¿notice of entry of judgment… The memorandum of costs must be verified by a statement of the party, attorney, or agent that to the best of his or her knowledge the items of cost are correct and were necessarily incurred in the case.”  (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1700.) 

The losing party may contest the costs that a prevailing party seeks.  (Code Civ. Proc., §1034(a).)  The challenging party has the burden of demonstrating that those costs are unreasonable or unnecessary. (Adams v. Ford Motor Co.,¿(2011) 199 Cal. App. 4th 1475, 1486; 612¿South LLC v. Laconic Limited Partnership, (2010) 184 Cal. App. 4th 1270, 1285.)  

Code Civ. Proc. § 1033.5 sets forth the costs recoverable by the prevailing party. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1033.5.)  “Allowable costs shall be reasonably necessary to the conduct of the litigation rather than merely convenient or beneficial to its preparation.”  (Code Civ. Proc., §1033.5(c)(2); Perko’s Enterprises, Inc. v. RRNS Enterprises (l992) 4 Cal.App.4th 238, 244.)  A “properly verified memorandum of costs is considered prima facie evidence that the costs listed in the memorandum were necessarily incurred.”  (Bach v. County of Butte (1989) 215 Cal.App.3d 294, 308; see also Hadley v. Krepel (1985) 167 Cal.App.3d 677, 682.)   

This puts the burden on the party seeking to tax costs to show that they were not reasonable or necessary.  (Ladas v. California State Automotive Assoc. (1993) 19 Cal.App.4th 761, 773-74.)  If items are properly objected to, they are put in issue, and the burden of proof is on the party claiming them as costs. (Id.) 

The memorandum of costs need not contain invoices, billings, or statements.  (Bach, 215 Cal.App.3d at 308; see also Cal. Rules of Court, Rule 3.1700(a)(1) (only verification required).) “Documentation must be submitted only when a party dissatisfied with the costs claimed in the memorandum challenges them by filing a motion to tax costs.”  (Bach, 215 Cal.App.3d at 308.)     

DISCUSSION  

As a threshold matter, Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider allowing Defendant to file a late opposition.  Plaintiff’s motion to tax/strike costs was originally noticed for hearing on August 21, 2026.  The motion was served by email on Defendant through One Legal.  Opposition papers were due nine court days before that hearing, or on August 10, 2026. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1005, subd. (b).)  Defendant did not file an opposition by August 10.  

At the hearing on the motion, Defendant’s counsel represented that he was not served with the motion.  According to Defendant, he does not receive motions or papers served through One Legal, because they are diverted to his spam or updates, and he previously informed Plaintiff he does not receive documents served by One Legal.  Based on this representation, the Court continued the hearing on the motion to strike to allow Defendant to file an opposition. 

In reply, Plaintiff presents evidence of One Legal’s records which show that defense counsel was able to retrieve and view other documents served through One Legal, including the request for dismissal which triggered the timeline for Defendant to file its memorandum of costs.  Based on this new evidence, the Court reverses its grant of leave to Defendant to file a late opposition.  Defendant cannot rely on One Legal service to claim its costs and simultaneously tell the Court that One Legal service does not reach it.   

Defendant’s opposition, therefore, was late, and the Court has discretion to disregard a late-filed opposition, which it does so here.  The effect of the Court’s ruling to disregard Defendant’s late-filed opposition is that Defendant has not submitted invoices to support the costs challenged.  Once claimed costs are challenged, it is the obligation of the claiming party to provide documentation to establish the veracity, reasonableness and/or necessity of the costs claimed.  (Jones v. Dumrichob (1998) 63 Cal.App.4th 1258, 1267.)  Accordingly, the costs will be taxed.   

CONCLUSION 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS the motion to tax costs. 

 

IT IS SO ORDERED. 

 

DATED:  September 14, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

Case Number: 23SMCV05886    Hearing Date: September 14, 2026    Dept: 205

Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District 

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

PRECISE GENERAL CONTRACTOR, INC.,  

  

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

BLACKBRIAR DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 23SMCV05886 

  

  Date: September 14, 2026 

  

  ORDER RE: 

  BLACKBRIAR DEVELOPMENT AND  

  JOELLE RIMOKH’S MOTION  

  FOR LEAVE TO FILE CROSS- 

  COMPLAINT  

   

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This case arises from a dispute between a general contractor and a subcontractor.  Plaintiff Precise General Contractor Inc. entered into a written agreement with Defendant Blackbriar Development Corporation for drywall work relating to real property located in Beverly Hills (the “Property”).  Precise sued Blackbriar, claiming it failed to pay invoices of over $168,000.   

The operative complaint alleges claims of (1) breach of contract, (2) foreclosure on mechanic’s lien, (3) recovery on mechanic’s lien release bond, (4) recovery on contractor’s license bond, (5) open book account, (6) account stated, (7) quantum meruit, and (8) prompt payment penalties.  Blackbriar filed an answer without any cross-claims.   

This hearing is on Blackbriar’s motion for leave to file cross-complaint.  Blackbriar seeks to recover losses associated with having to hire a replacement contractor as a result of Precise’s alleged partial and defective performance.  Blackbriar also seeks to add Western Surety Corporation, which issued a contractor’s bond to Precise.   

Blackbriar claims it did not include these cross-claims at the time it filed its answer because it could not yet determine whether or the extent to which, Precise’s failure to complete the project damaged Blackbriar.  Blackbriar has finished Precise’s work and is now able to quantify its damages against Precise.  Blackbriar seeks leave to add claims for (1) breach of contract, (2) negligence, (3) disgorgement and (4) on contractors’ license bond.   

Precise has filed a limited and late opposition to the motion for leave to file cross-complaint.  Precise argues that it did not file a timely opposition because at the time its opposition was due, it believed that the Court would grant the parties’ stipulation to continue the trial and trial related deadlines.  The Court denied the stipulation after Precise’s deadline to file an opposition had passed, and now that there is no continuance,  

Precise argues it will be prejudiced by the amendment because it (and Blackbriar) will have limited time to conduct discovery on the new claims.  Precise argues that if the Court is inclined to grant the motion for leave to file the cross-complaint, the Court should vacate its prior ruling and continue the trial and trial-related dates.  Precise seeks a 10-month continuance to September 2, 2027.  Alternatively, Precise asks the Court to impose “such other terms or case-management measures” as will prevent the prejudice to the parties.   

LEGAL STANDARDS 

Code of Civil Procedure section 428.10, subdivision (b), authorizes a party against whom a cause of action has been asserted to file a cross-complaint alleging a cause of action against a person alleged to be liable thereon, whether or not that person is already a party, when the proposed cause of action “(1) arises out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences as the cause brought against him or (2) asserts a claim, right, or interest in the property or controversy which is the subject of the cause brought against him.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.10, subd. (b).)  

A party may file a cross-complaint against a co-party or another person before the court sets a trial date. (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50(b).)  Here, trial has already been set (for November 2, 2026.)  Once a trial date has been set, the party must obtain leave of court, which “may be granted in the interest of justice at any time during the course of the action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50(c).)  

DISCUSSION 

Code of Civil Procedure section 426.50 governs compulsory counterclaims.  It states: “A party who fails to plead a cause of action subject to the requirements of this article [on compulsory cross-complaints], whether through oversight, inadvertence, mistake, neglect, or other cause, may apply to the court for leave … to file a cross-complaint, to assert such cause at any time during the course of the action. The court … shall grant … leave … to file the cross-complaint, to assert such cause if the party who failed to plead the cause acted in good faith. This subdivision shall be liberally construed to avoid forfeiture of causes of action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 426.50.) 

If the proposed cross-claims are compulsory, then leave must be granted unless there is “substantial evidence” of “bad faith of the moving party,” i.e., “dishonest purpose, moral obliquity, sinister motive, furtive design or ill will.” (Silver Organizations Ltd. v. Frank (1990) 217 Cal.App.3d 94, 98-100; see Code Civ. Proc., §§ 426.10, subd. (c), 426.50.) This reflects the policy against forfeiture of causes of action, because compulsory-cross-claims cannot be asserted in any subsequent action brought by the putative cross-complainant against the plaintiff; they must be asserted in the action initiated by the plaintiff or else they are forfeited. (Code Civ. Pro. section 426.30.)  

A compulsory counterclaim is “a claim tending to diminish the plaintiff's recovery; it must permit a several judgment between the parties; and it must arise out of the same ‘transaction’ as that which produced the plaintiff's original action. This claim is often described as a ‘transaction counterclaim.’”  (Ranchers Bank v. Pressman (1971) 19 Cal.App.3d 612, 620.)  A compulsory counterclaim must exist at the time of the filing of the complaint. 

Code of Civil Procedure section 428.10¿governs permissive cross-complaints. It provides in relevant part: “A party against whom a cause of action has been asserted . . .¿may¿file a cross-complaint setting forth [¶] . . . [¶] (b) Any cause of action he has against¿a person¿alleged to be liable thereon,¿whether or not such person is already a party to the action, if the cause of action asserted in his cross-complaint (1) arises out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences as the cause brought against him.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.10, subd. (b), italics added.)   

If the proposed cross-claims are permissive, then leave should be granted “in the interests of justice.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50, subd. (c).) “Unless it would interfere with the trial date or otherwise prejudice the action, courts are inclined to grant leave to file [a permissive] cross-complaint against the plaintiff.” (Weil & Brown, Cal. Practice Guide: Civil Procedure Before Trial (The Rutter Group 2023) ¶ 6:564.) This “reflects the judicial policy of settling all disputes between plaintiff and defendant in the same lawsuit if possible.” (Ibid.) 

Here, Blackbriar’s proposed cross-complaint against Precise is a compulsory cross-complaint because it arises from the same transaction as the complaint – namely Precise’s alleged defective drywall work on the Property.  Where the cross-complaint is compulsory, the Court is required to grant leave to amend unless there is substantial evidence of bad faith on the part of moving party.  (Silver Organizations Ltd. v. Frank (1990) 217 Cal.App.3d 94, 98-100.) 

“Substantial evidence” is evidence “of ponderable legal significance, . . . reasonable in nature, credible, and of solid value.” (Bowers¿v.¿Bernards¿(1984) 150 Cal.App.3d 870, 873, italics in original.) “Bad faith” involves “actual or constructive fraud, or a design to mislead or deceive another, or a neglect or refusal to fulfill some duty or some contractual obligation, not prompted by an honest mistake . . ., but by some interested or sinister motive[,] . . . not simply bad judgment or negligence, but rather¿. . . the conscious doing of a wrong because of dishonest purpose or moral obliquity; . . . it contemplates a state of mind affirmatively operating with furtive design or ill will. [Citation.]' [Citations.]” (Pugh¿v.¿See's¿Candies, Inc. (1988) 203 Cal.App.3d 743, 764.)   

Blackbriar has filed a declaration from its CEO and President stating that Blackbriar did not file the cross-claims earlier because it had not yet determined if it was damaged at all by Precise’s defective performance.  There is no evidence of any dishonest purpose or fraud on the part of Blackbriar.   

Plaintiff’s limited opposition claims that it will be prejudiced by the filing of the proposed cross-complaint because it will not have an opportunity to conduct discovery as trial is set to start on November 2, 2026.   Courts have held that bad faith may be shown by evidence of delay that would work a substantial injustice to the opposing party and would prejudice that party’s position in some way.  (Foot’s Transfer & Storage Co. v. Superior Court (1980) 114 Cal.App.3d 897, 904 (citing Gherman v. Colburn (1977) 72 Cal.App.3d 544, 559.)  There is no evidence of a delay.  Accordingly, the Court must grant Blackbriar leave to file the cross-complaint against Precise.  

As to Western, the cross-complaint is permissive as Western is not currently a party in this action.  “Permission to file a permissive cross-complaint is solely within the trial court’s discretion.” (Crocker Nat. Bank. v. Emerald¿(1990) 221 Cal.App.3d 852, 864; see¿Orient Handel v. United States Fid. & Guar. Co.¿(1987) 192 Cal.App.3d 684, 701.) ¿Factors¿considered are judicial efficiency, fairness to the parties, the interests of justice, and delay in seeking court's permission to file the cross-complaint.¿(Crocker, 221 Cal.App.3d at 864.) 

Here, judicial efficiency supports trying the proposed cross-claims against Western Surety with the main action.  Precise seeks compensation for its work.  Blackbriar alleges the work was defective, and in fact, it is entitled to sue Precise’s bond company for damages incurred due to Precise’s willful and deliberate violations of the contractor’s license law.   

Blackbriar does not clearly say when it first obtained knowledge of Precise’s alleged violations of the contractors license law.  The proposed cross-complaint does not even clearly state what Precise did to violate the contractor’s license law.  It simply cites to several statutes (Business and Professions Code §§7108, 7108.5, 7109, and 7120) which deal with the diversion and misuse of progress payments and failure to keep accurate records.   

Further, trial is less than two months away, and Western Surety has not been involved in this action including obtaining discovery relating to whether it has defenses based on the validity or existence of the claim, possible breach of contract or fault of Precise, non-compliance with bond conditions, scope of coverage defenses and other procedural and statutory defenses.   

On these facts, the Court would normally deny leave to file because both Western and Plaintiff would be prejudiced by the addition of Western Surety.  However, any prejudice may be mitigated by a continuance.   

Precise proposes a 10-month continuance to September 12, 2027.  The Court will grant a continuance to September 13, 2027 at 8:30 a.m. (September 12 is a Sunday).  The Final Status Conference is continued to September 13, 2027 at 8:30 a.m.   Should the parties require a further continuance, they may file a motion to continue trial.       

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

    For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS the motion for leave to file a cross-complaint against Precise and Western Surety, and continues the trial and all trial related deadlines.  The trial is continued to September 13, 2027, and the final status conference is continued to September 3, 2027. 
IT IS SO ORDERED.
